a lizard able to change skin colour, ranked among unclean animals (Lev. 11:30).
likely the wild sheep, an animal permitted as food under the Mosaic law (Deut. 14:5).
the single combatant representing an army, as Goliath before the Israelite and Philistine camps (1 Sam. 17:4).
Scripture teaches there is no true chance in God's providence; apparent coincidence is really the outworking of his plan (Luke 10:31).
a Persian title for a provincial governor with judicial authority (Ezra 4:8).
additional garments reckoned among the treasures of wealthy men (Gen. 45:22).
the bed of a sea or river (Ps. 18:15), or, in Job 31:22, the collarbone.
a sanctuary, used once contemptuously of Bethel as "the king's chapel" (Amos 7:13).
the ornamental capital of a pillar (1 Kings 7:16).
the ancient and modern divisions of Scripture into chapters, standardized by Cardinal Hugo of St. Cher around A.D. 1240.
"craftsmen," a valley named in 1 Chr. 4:14, otherwise unknown.
a bowl or deep dish; the one presenting John the Baptist's head was a flat platter (Matt. 14:8).
a vehicle chiefly for war, first mentioned with Joseph's honour in Egypt, later used extensively by Israel's kings from Solomon onward; Elijah was translated in "a chariot of fire" (2 Kings 2:11).
the Authorized Version's rendering of the Greek word for love, the greatest of the Christian graces (1 Cor. 13).
one who practises serpent-charming or enchantment (Ps. 58:5; Deut. 18:11).
another form of Haran (Acts 7:2).
a river in the land of the Chaldeans where exiled Jews, including Ezekiel, were settled (Ezek. 1:1-3).
the king of Elam who invaded Canaan in Abraham's time and was defeated by Abraham's small force after taking Lot captive (Gen. 14).
smiting on the cheek was accounted a grievous insult; "turning the other cheek" (Luke 6:29) teaches non-resistance of evil.
curd or curdled milk, mentioned three times under different Hebrew words (1 Sam. 17:18; 2 Sam. 17:29; Job 10:10).
idolatrous priests (Zeph. 1:4), possibly meaning those who prostrate themselves before idols.
the national god of the Moabites, whose worship Solomon introduced at Jerusalem and Josiah abolished (1 Kings 11:7; 2 Kings 23:13).
merchant, the name of a Benjamite and of the father of a false prophet.
"chief of the Levites" under David, probably a Kohathite (1 Chr. 15:22).
a Gibeonite Hivite city with which Joshua made a league, belonging to Benjamin (Josh. 9:17).
more often Cherethites, inhabitants of southern Philistia who with the Pelethites formed David's bodyguard (1 Sam. 30:14; 2 Sam. 8:18).
the brook where Elijah hid during the drought, fed by ravens (1 Kings 17:3-5).
plural cherubim, symbolic composite figures guarding Eden and forming the throne and chariot of God's presence over the ark's mercy-seat (Gen. 3:24; Ex. 25:17-22).
a place on the border of Judah (Josh. 15:10).
the son of Nahor (Gen. 22:22).
a town in southern Judah, probably the same as Bethul (Josh. 15:30).
a coffer for temple contributions, rendered "ark" or "coffin" elsewhere (2 Kings 12:9; Gen. 50:26).
likely the Oriental plane tree, which sheds its bark annually, mentioned in Jacob's dealings with Laban's flocks (Gen. 30:37).
a town of Issachar, identified with Chisloth-tabor (Josh. 19:18).
the town where Shelah, son of Judah, was born, probably the same as Achzib (Gen. 38:5).
the threshing-floor where Uzzah died for touching the ark, called Nachon's threshing-floor in 2 Sam. 6:6 (1 Chr. 13:9).
a title given to Adino the Eznite, one of David's greatest heroes, also called Jashobeam (2 Sam. 23:8).
see Priest.
"Asiarchs," wealthy officials who presided over religious festivals and games in the cities of proconsular Asia (Acts 19:31).
a word with wide latitude in Scripture, applied even to adults; figuratively used of the ignorant or narrow-minded, and of simplicity and humility as Christ commended in children.
David's second son by Abigail, also called Daniel, who apparently died young (2 Sam. 3:3).
the younger son of Elimelech and Naomi, husband of Orpah (Ruth 1:2).
an unknown place or country that traded with Tyre (Ezek. 27:23).
probably the youngest son of Barzillai, to whom David gave a possession at Bethlehem as reward for his father's loyalty (2 Sam. 19:37-40).
a fenced city near the Sea of Galilee that gave its name to the lake, later called the Sea of Galilee or Tiberias (Deut. 3:17).
an island in the Aegean Sea where Paul anchored on his third missionary return journey (Acts 20:15).
the third civil (ninth ecclesiastical) Jewish month, corresponding roughly to November (Neh. 1:1).
or Kittim, descendants of Javan, probably denoting Cyprus and later the islands and coasts of the Mediterranean generally (Gen. 10:4; Num. 24:24).
an idol mentioned in Amos 5:26, likely representing the planet Saturn, to which the Phoenicians offered human sacrifices.
a Christian woman whose household informed Paul of divisions in the Corinthian church (1 Cor. 1:11).
a place David and his men frequented, probably identical with Ashan (1 Sam. 30:30).
a city near Capernaum where Christ's mighty works were done but which was doomed for its unbelief (Matt. 11:21).
used of warriors, the Hebrew nation, Jerusalem, Christ, and the apostles; "many are called, but few are chosen" refers to those who fail to profit from their opportunities (Matt. 20:16).
the same as Chezib and Achzib, a place in the Judean lowlands (1 Chr. 4:22).

"anointed," the Greek translation of "Messiah," the official title of Jesus as Prophet, Priest, and King, occurring over 500 times in the New Testament, fulfilling the Old Testament's prophetic portrait of the promised Deliverer.
the name given, probably in reproach, to Christ's followers, first used at Antioch, occurring only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26).
persons who have falsely claimed to be the Messiah, as Christ warned would arise (Matt. 24:24).
"the words of the days," the daily or yearly records of a kingdom's transactions, recorded in order of time.

originally one book, covering genealogies and the reigns of David and Solomon and the subsequent kingdom of Judah to the Exile, likely compiled by Ezra after the Exile from public records and earlier writings, emphasizing ecclesiastical over political history.
statistical state records that were among the sources used by the compiler of Chronicles (1 Chr. 27:24).

the arrangement of biblical events in order of time, complicated by differing systems (Hebrew, Septuagint, Samaritan) for the patriarchal period and by Ussher's and Hales's differing modern calculations.
a greenish-golden precious stone (Rev. 21:20).
a people allied with Egypt in Nebuchadnezzar's time, probably of Northern Africa (Ezek. 30:5).
a city of Hadarezer from which David took bronze for the temple, called Berothai elsewhere (1 Chr. 18:8).

from Greek ecclesia ("assembly"), used in the New Testament for a local congregation, all Christians in a city, or the whole body of the redeemed (the invisible church); marked by unity, universality, and perpetuity, and continuous with the Old Testament people of God.
a coarse, ill-natured, or deceiving person (1 Sam. 25:3).
the king of Mesopotamia who oppressed Israel in the generation after Joshua (Judg. 3:8).
a maritime province of south-east Asia Minor, home of Tarsus and Paul, famous for goat's-hair cloth used in tentmaking.
an aromatic spice from a Laurel-family tree of India and Ceylon, an ingredient of the holy anointing oil (Ex. 30:23).
a fenced city and district of Naphtali near the lake later called Gennesaret (Josh. 19:35).
used of the sun's apparent revolution and the changes of the wind (Ps. 19:6; Eccl. 1:6).

the covenant rite instituted with Abraham as the sign of Israel's consecration to God, obligatory for all Hebrew males and their household servants, continued until superseded by baptism under the New Testament, though some Jewish Christians wrongly sought to impose it on Gentile converts.
a receptacle for collected rainwater, distinguished from a natural spring; empty cisterns were sometimes used as prisons (Jer. 38:6).
rights and privileges distinguishing a citizen from a foreigner; Roman citizenship, which Paul possessed, guaranteed protection from arbitrary imprisonment or scourging (Acts 22:25-28).

urban settlement first mentioned with Cain's founding of Enoch; cities of refuge and fenced cities with walls and towers are described throughout the Old Testament; Jerusalem is called "the Holy City."
a small island off south-west Crete passed by Paul on his voyage to Rome (Acts 27:16).
a Christian woman mentioned by Paul, possibly a British princess (2 Tim. 4:21).
(1.) The fourth Roman emperor, who banished the Jews (and Christians) from Rome about A.D. 49 (Acts 18:2). (2.) Claudius Lysias, a Roman officer who rescued Paul at Jerusalem (Acts 21:31-40).
used of sediment, potter's material, and sealing substance; Christ's tomb may have been sealed with clay (Matt. 27:66).

the Mosaic distinction between clean and unclean animals and substances, existing before the Flood and regulated in detail by the law of Moses, designed partly to distinguish Israel from other nations.
a Christian of Philippi, Paul's "fellow-labourer," possibly identified with Clement of Rome (Phil. 4:3).
one of the two disciples who met the risen Christ on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:18).
the Aramaic form Clopas, possibly the same as Alphaeus, husband of the Mary mentioned in John 19:25.
an outer garment worn by priests, kings, and others of rank; the Roman traveling cloak Paul left at Troas (2 Tim. 4:13) was called the paenula.
a storehouse, and hence a place of privacy for prayer (Matt. 6:6).

used as a symbol of the Divine presence and glory (the Shechinah), of transitory things, and of Christ's second coming "in the clouds"; the pillar of cloud led Israel through the wilderness by day and became fire by night.
a town and harbour in Asia Minor passed by Paul on his voyage to Rome (Acts 27:7).
the Hebrews' common fuel was dried dung and wood charcoal rather than mineral coal; "coals of fire" is used figuratively of divine judgment and of overcoming evil with kindness (Rom. 12:20).
the tunic worn next to the skin, sometimes woven without seam (John 19:23) or of "many colours" as Joseph's coat (Gen. 37:3).
armor of glittering scales, also called a habergeon or brigandine (1 Sam. 17:5).
a fabulous serpent, likely denoting the cerastes or another dangerous viper (Isa. 11:8).
in Christ's time this term, along with the Roman four-watch division of the night, marked a recognized time signal, referenced in the Gospels' accounts of Peter's denial.
a noisome weed, possibly darnel or "tares" (Job 31:40).
"hollow Syria," the Greek name for the valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges.
the small box in which the Philistines placed their trespass-offering beside the ark (1 Sam. 6:8).
used of Joseph's burial, referring to an Egyptian mummy-chest (Gen. 50:26).
earnest thoughts or meditations (Dan. 7:28).
before the Exile the Jews used weighed, uncoined silver rather than stamped money; the shekel was the standard unit of value.
the neck-opening of a garment (Job 30:18); also used of ear-pendants taken as spoil from the Midianites (Judg. 8:26).
the pecuniary contributions Paul gathered from Gentile churches for poor Christians in Palestine (Rom. 15:25-26; 1 Cor. 16:1-3).
properly "the second quarter" of Jerusalem, the residence of the prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22:14).
Philippi was a Roman colony, a military settlement of Roman citizens governed under Roman municipal law (Acts 16:12).
a city of Phrygia on the Lycus, whose church was probably founded by Epaphras and to which Paul wrote his epistle without having personally visited it.

written by Paul from Rome during his first imprisonment (about A.D. 57 or 62) to counteract false teaching combining Oriental mysticism with Christianity, emphasizing Christ's supremacy (doctrinal, chs. 1-2) and its practical implications (chs. 3-4).

white symbolized purity, joy, and victory; black, mourning and calamity; red, bloodshed; purple and blue, royalty; scarlet, wealth and luxury; these colours featured prominently in the tabernacle curtains and priestly garments.
the designation of the Holy Spirit (Gr. paracletos, properly "Advocate"), one summoned to plead a cause on another's behalf (John 14:16).
refers either to his first advent or his promised second coming at the last day, and is used metaphorically of the spread of the gospel and the establishment of his kingdom.
the Decalogue, given to Israel at Sinai and written by God on two tables of stone, summarizing the immutable moral law, divided differently among Jewish, Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed traditions.
fellowship with God and between believers, including the Lord's Supper, so named for the fellowship it signifies between Christ and his disciples (1 Cor. 10:16-17).
a Levite placed over temple tithes (2 Chr. 35:9).
Paul's contemptuous term ("mutilation") for those who pressed circumcision on Gentile converts (Phil. 3:2).
a wife of secondary rank recognized and regulated but not fully protected under Mosaic law, a practice ended by Christian teaching restoring marriage to its original character.
evil desire or coveting (Rom. 7:8; Col. 3:5).
a water channel; Hezekiah's conduit conveyed water from the upper pool into Jerusalem in preparation for siege (2 Kings 20:20).
the rock hyrax, a small, gregarious animal living in rock clefts, described in Scripture as "exceeding wise" though feeble (Prov. 30:24-26).
a perfume compound (Ex. 30:35).
perfumers who compounded spices and perfumes (1 Sam. 8:13).
an open profession of faith, or an acknowledgment of sin to God and to a wronged neighbour (Luke 12:8; James 5:16).
the Hebrew people collectively as a holy community, summoned by trumpet to the tabernacle door for religious assemblies (Num. 10:3); later represented by the Sanhedrim.
(Isa. 14:13), likely the northern mountain the Babylonians regarded as the meeting-place of their gods, spoken from the perspective of the king of Babylon.
the inborn faculty for judging right and wrong, common to all people but perverted by the Fall, which believers are urged to keep "void of offence" (Acts 24:16).
the setting apart of persons or things to God's service, as with the tribe of Levi and the firstborn under Mosaic law, and all Christians under the New Testament (1 Pet. 2:9).
a common Jewish title for the Messiah, drawn from Isaiah's prophecies of comfort (Luke 2:25).
a recognized cluster of stars; in Isa. 13:10 the Hebrew word denotes the constellation Orion, associated with Nimrod as a symbol of impiety.
a state of mind confined to one's lot, opposed to envy, avarice, ambition, and anxiety, rooted in humility and trust in providence (1 Tim. 6:6).
one's manner of life or conduct, not verbal communication, in its biblical usage (Eph. 4:22).
the turning of a sinner to God, whether in the general sense of abandoning false religion or the deeper sense of a life transformed by divine grace (Acts 15:3; 26:18).
a religious assembly distinct from the more general congregation, as on the Sabbath and the annual feasts, called a "holy convocation" (Lev. 23).
in early times cooking was done by the mistress of the household; professional cooks appear later (1 Sam. 8:13).
a small Aegean island where Paul stopped after leaving Miletus (Acts 21:1).
the metal usually mistranslated "brass" in the Authorized Version, abundant in Palestine and used for tabernacle and temple vessels and weapons.
a Hebrew measure equal to one homer, containing ten ephahs or ten baths (Ezek. 45:14).
a marine calcareous formation, valued especially in its red form for ornaments (Job 28:18).
a Hebrew word for anything irrevocably dedicated to God, which the Pharisees misused as a device to avoid supporting their parents, condemned by Christ (Mark 7:11).
used literally for fastening tents and binding prisoners, and figuratively of death, sorrow, sin's consequences, and union ("a threefold cord," Eccl. 4:12).
an umbelliferous plant whose seed, resembling a small ball, is likened to manna in form and colour (Ex. 16:31).

a wealthy Grecian city on the isthmus joining the Peloponnesus to the mainland, rebuilt by the Romans and known for luxury and immorality; Paul resided there eighteen months, and it hosted a large mixed church of Jews and Gentiles (Acts 18:1-18).

written by Paul from Ephesus (about A.D. 57) after reports of factions, immorality, and doctrinal confusion in the Corinthian church, addressing divisions (chs. 1-4), moral abuses (5-6), doctrinal questions including the Lord's Supper (7-14), and the resurrection (15-16).

written by Paul, probably from Macedonia (about A.D. 58), after Titus brought encouraging news from Corinth, discussing his ministry and affection for them (1-7), the collection for Judean believers (8-9), and a defense of his apostolic authority (10-13).
an unclean plunging seabird (Lev. 11:17), possibly the same word elsewhere rendered "pelican."
a general term for grain of various kinds, an important article of Hebrew diet and, from Solomon's time, an export commodity.
a devout Roman centurion at Caesarea whose household became the first Gentile converts, baptized by Peter (Acts 10).
used of the angle of a building or street and figuratively of a whole territory ("four corners of the earth"); Christ is called "the corner stone" set in highest honour (Matt. 21:42).
a musical horn, usually rendered "trumpet," sounded at festivals including the preparation for the Day of Atonement (1 Chr. 15:28).
pens or enclosures for flocks (2 Chr. 32:28).
a temporary shed or booth used by watchmen in vineyards or gardens, removed when no longer needed (Isa. 1:8).
a seat for rest or repose (Job 7:13).
a ploughshare or facing-piece of a plough (1 Sam. 13:20-21).
the Jewish Sanhedrim, the supreme national tribunal, with subordinate local courts; in church history the word denotes assemblies of bishops or pastors, the first being that of Acts 15.
an adviser, used of royal advisers and, once, of the Messiah (Isa. 9:6).
the twenty-four divisions David organized among priests, singers, and other Levites for rotating temple service (1 Chr. 24-26), reestablished after the Exile by Ezra.
the enclosure of the tabernacle, temple, a prison, or a private house or palace.

a solemn agreement, used of compacts between people and, especially, of God's gracious self-revealing promises to Noah, Abraham, and Israel at Sinai; theologians distinguish the "covenant of works" made with Adam and the "covenant of grace," the eternal plan of redemption fulfilled through Christ.
occurs in Gen. 20:16, likely an implied instruction for Sarah to wear a veil as married women did.
a strong desire for worldly possessions, condemned throughout Scripture (Col. 3:5; 1 Tim. 6:9-10).
a cow and her calf were not to be slaughtered on the same day (Lev. 22:28).
a migratory bird known for its loud, melancholy cry (Isa. 38:14).

God's free act of calling all things into being out of nothing "in the beginning," attributed throughout Scripture to the Godhead, the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, with the chief end being the manifestation of God's glory.
denotes the whole created order or the whole human race depending on context (Rom. 8:39; Mark 16:15).
one of Paul's assistants, possibly a Christian of Rome (2 Tim. 4:10).
a large Mediterranean island whose people Paul described as characteristically deceitful (Titus 1:12); visited by Paul en route to Rome, where he later left Titus to organize the church.
see Colour.
a female ornament, probably a reticule or pouch (Isa. 3:22).
the chief of the synagogue at Corinth, converted and baptized by Paul (Acts 18:8).
the instrument of Roman crucifixion, and by extension a term for Christ's crucifixion itself and for any severe affliction; the Latin cross (crux immissa) was the form used for Christ.

worn as a symbol of royal or priestly office, honour, victory, or festivity in the ancient Near East and in Greek and Roman games; believers are promised an "incorruptible crown" or "crown of life" (James 1:12).
placed on Christ in mockery by Roman soldiers, probably woven from the thorny nabk shrub common around Jerusalem (Matt. 27:29).

a horrific form of capital punishment among heathen nations, likely not practised by ancient Jews, involving scourging and carrying one's own cross; Christ's unusually rapid death was attributed to his intense mental anguish rather than mere physical exhaustion.
a small vessel for water or oil (1 Sam. 26:11; 1 Kings 17:12).
a clear quartz stone described as dazzling in Ezekiel's vision and Revelation (Ezek. 1:22; Rev. 4:6).
a measure of length based on the forearm, commonly about 20.24 inches, with a "sacred cubit" slightly longer.
a bird mentioned among the unclean species, possibly a seagull or petrel rather than the true cuckoo (Lev. 11:16).
a widely cultivated vegetable of the gourd family, longed for by the Israelites in the wilderness as a reminder of Egypt (Num. 11:5).
an aromatic seed used as a spice and tithed scrupulously by the Pharisees while they neglected weightier matters (Matt. 23:23).
a wine-vessel, often of gold among the wealthy, used figuratively of one's lot in life ("cup of salvation," "cup of trembling") and, at the Last Supper, of the sacramental "cup of blessing."
a high-ranking royal officer responsible for the king's wine, such as Pharaoh's cupbearer and Nehemiah under Artaxerxes.
magical practices and charms sold by Ephesian sorcerers, whose books were publicly burned by new converts (Acts 19:19).
divine or prophetic maledictions pronounced against sin, distinct from personal cursing (which was forbidden and, against God, punishable by death), as in the curses on the serpent and Cain.

the linen and goat's-hair coverings of the tabernacle, and the veil (a different Hebrew word) separating the holy of holies; used figuratively of the heavens spread out like a tent-awning (Isa. 40:22).

black. (1.) A son of Ham and father of Nimrod, from whom the land of Cush (likely including regions in both Arabia and Africa/Ethiopia) took its name. (2.) A Benjamite mentioned in the title of Psalm 7.
likely a poetic name for the land of Cush, possibly linked to Chushan-rishathaim (Hab. 3:7).
used of several individuals, including the messenger who told David of Absalom's death (2 Sam. 18:32), and of the foreign wife Moses married (Num. 12:1).
a Roman tax collected by publicans, who were widely hated for their extortion; a separate half-shekel temple tax was paid annually by Jewish men in Jewish coin, requiring money-changers.
a Babylonian city or district from which colonists were transplanted to Samaria (2 Kings 17:24).
self-laceration was an idolatrous mourning practice forbidden to the Israelites (Lev. 19:28), though grief-driven tearing of flesh was sometimes regarded as a mark of affection.
percussion instruments of two brass plates clashed together to produce a loud sound, used in temple worship (1 Chr. 13:8).
an evergreen tree with hard, fragrant, durable wood, associated with funerals and mourning (Isa. 44:14).
a large Mediterranean island, the Old Testament "Chittim," birthplace of Barnabas and scene of Paul's first missionary labours with Barnabas and John Mark (Acts 13:4-13).
a North African city with a large Jewish population; Simon, who bore Christ's cross, was a native, and Cyrenian believers helped found the Gentile church at Antioch (Matt. 27:32; Acts 11:20).
the Grecized form of Quirinus, governor of Syria (via Cilicia) at the time of the census associated with Christ's birth (Luke 2:2).
the Persian king who conquered Babylon (B.C. 538) and issued the decree permitting the Jews to return and rebuild Jerusalem, a major turning point in Jewish history (Ezra 1:1-4).
